segments.text: A snake flicks its tongue in and out.
Its nose just breathes - the tongue does the smelling.
Each flick picks up scent particles from the air.
The two forked tips touch separate detectors in the roof of its mouth.
Each side picks up a different strength of scent.
The stronger side points toward the prey.
That detector is called the Jacobson's organ.
It turns that way to track the prey.
Flicking its tongue is how a snake smells out which way to go.
